lesson_title: Velcro, Magnets and Handshakes: Why Molecules Boil When They Do
hook_text: Butane and propan-1-ol weigh almost the same. One boils below zero. The other at 97 degrees. Why?
clip_script: Two molecules, almost identical in mass. Butane boils at minus 0,5 degrees — it's a gas before your kettle even starts. Propan-1-ol, the same size, boils at 97,2. What's going on? Every molecule is wearing velcro — weak little London forces that every molecule owns. Longer molecule, longer strip, more grip: that's why boiling points climb up the alkane family. Crumple the molecule with branches and the strips can't lie flat against each other — grip drops, boiling point drops. But some molecules carry upgrades. Aldehydes and ketones have fridge magnets — a positive end and a negative end snapping molecules together. And alcohols? Alcohols shake hands. A hydrogen bonded straight onto an oxygen grabs the next molecule's oxygen — the hydrogen bond, strongest grip in the syllabus. That handshake is the whole difference between butane's minus 0,5 and propan-1-ol's 97,2. Carboxylic acids shake with BOTH hands and top every chart. So next time a bottle of nail polish remover empties itself overnight, you know the secret: weak grip, easy escape, high vapour pressure. Strong grip, high boiling point. One idea — the whole topic.
visual_style: Molecules as figures wearing velcro strips lying flat against each other, then crumpling into balls that barely touch; upgrade icons appearing — a magnet clicking on, two hands clasping — beside a rising boiling-point thermometer.
mood: Curious and tactile — invisible forces made touchable.
pacing: Puzzle opening with the two thermometers, three quick upgrade beats, satisfying single-idea close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and explain any boiling point in the paper in four sentences.
